question: Why does a dime have ridges, but a nickel doesn't?
notes: Narration v5. Times are seconds into voice.mp3, computed from words.json by shots.py. Each scene is one stop on the vertical paper strip. "paint" lists where the red-lead paint lands and the word it lands on. Real US coins: dime 17.9 mm, nickel 21.2 mm.

scenes.line: Why does a dime have ridges, but a nickel doesn't?

art.desc: A dime and a nickel on edge, side by side: the dime ridged, the nickel smooth (true size ratio 17.9 : 21.2)

scenes.line: Those ridges, and some bricked-up windows in England, trace back to the same crime.

art.desc: A plain Georgian house front with two windows bricked up

scenes.line: Silver coins used to be worth their silver. They were hammered out by hand, with uneven edges,

art.desc: Making a coin by hand: hammer, punch, coin on a little anvil
An old hand-struck coin with a lumpy, uneven edge

scenes.line: so people snipped a little off and melted the clippings down.

art.desc: A hand with shears snipping a sliver off a coin
A little melting ladle over a brazier, slivers inside

paint.on: the sliver, as it comes off
the ladle: the paint is the clippings

scenes.beat_note: The paint is the silver here: snipped off, then dropped into the ladle.

scenes.line: You could hang for clipping. People clipped anyway.

art.desc: A coil of rope on a peg (no noose, no figure)

scenes.beat_note: Calm, a touch grim. No figure.

scenes.line: By the 1690s, England's silver coins were missing nearly half their silver.

art.desc: A balance: a clipped coin rides high against a full weight

paint.on: the clipped coin in the high pan

scenes.line: So England called them in and struck new coins by machine, with ridged edges. Clip one of those, and anyone can tell.

art.desc: A machine-made coin on edge, ridged, with one notch cut in

scenes.line: For months, the old coins were taken back at full value, so their owners didn't lose out. That cost the government millions of pounds.

paint.on: the chest, filling it; it drains on "cost"

scenes.line: To help pay for that, Parliament taxed houses by their windows. Windows were easy to count from the street.

art.desc: The same house, all five windows open
A 1690s tax assessor from behind, ledger in hand, pointing up

scenes.line: Some owners bricked windows up, to pay less tax. A few of those blank windows are still there.

art.desc: A plain Georgian house front with two windows bricked up

scenes.beat_note: Callback to scene 2: the same house.

scenes.line: America's silver coins, dimes included, got ridges too. A nickel is mostly copper, never worth clipping, so it stayed smooth.

art.desc: A dime and a nickel on edge, side by side: the dime ridged, the nickel smooth (true size ratio 17.9 : 21.2)

paint.on: the nickel; it slides off on "smooth"

scenes.beat_note: Callback to scene 1, now answered. The paint slips off the smooth nickel on "stayed smooth".

scenes.line: The silver left the dime in 1965. The ridges stayed.

art.desc: A dime drawn large, its ridged edge showing (the copper core as a thin band)

paint.on: the dime, filling it; it drains out

scenes.beat_note: Echoes Short 01 ("The silver left the dime in 1965. The size stayed.")

scenes.line: And why is some old glass purple? That's another story.

art.desc: An old sash window with small panes of wavy old glass

scenes.beat_note: The tease: Short 03 is purple glass.
